III.1.title: Eight rows of dancers
III.1.reflection: The head of the Ji family had eight rows of dancers perform in his courtyard, a display reserved for the Son of Heaven. Confucius says: if he can bear to do this, what can he not bear to do? Book III opens with ritual as a matter of station, and with a family that has taken more than its place.
III.1.question: What small overreach, in someone you know or in yourself, told you something larger?

III.2.title: The wrong hymn
III.2.reflection: The three great families of Lu closed their sacrifices with a hymn written for the royal house, which speaks of princes assisting and the Son of Heaven solemn. Confucius asks what those words can mean in their halls. A text sung in the wrong place becomes a kind of lie.
III.2.question: Have you used words, at some occasion, that did not belong to it?

III.3.title: Rites without humanity
III.3.reflection: If a person is not humane, what is ritual to them? If a person is not humane, what is music to them? Legge renders ren here as "the virtues proper to humanity". Form depends on the heart that fills it.
III.3.question: Which of your habits of courtesy are still filled with feeling, and which have gone empty?

III.4.title: The root of ritual
III.4.reflection: Lin Fang asks what is fundamental in ceremonies. A great question, says the Master: in festivity, better frugal than lavish; in mourning, better deep grief than perfect detail. When in doubt, choose the inner over the outward.
III.4.question: At the last ceremony you attended, a wedding or a funeral, what mattered most?

III.5.title: Rulers among the tribes
III.5.reflection: Legge reads this as: the tribes of the east and north have their rulers, unlike the Chinese states, which are without them, a lament for the disorder of Confucius's own land. Other readers take it the opposite way, that the tribes even with rulers are not equal to the states without them. Both readings say something about how Zhou China saw its neighbours.
III.5.question: When you compare your own place with another, which way does the comparison usually run?

III.6.title: The sacrifice on Mount Tai
III.6.reflection: The Ji family head prepares to sacrifice to Mount Tai, a rite for the ruler of the state alone. Confucius asks Ran You, who served the family, whether he can stop it, and Ran You says he cannot. Will the mountain, Confucius asks, be less discerning than Lin Fang, who asked about the root of ritual?
III.6.question: When have you served someone and been unable to stop them doing wrong?

III.7.title: Contest with courtesy
III.7.reflection: The junzi does not compete, except perhaps in archery, and even there he bows to his opponent before and after, and drinks the forfeit with him. Legge keeps the Chinese word here: "Chun-tsze". The point is that rivalry can be held inside a form that respects the other side.
III.7.question: Where do you compete, and what form keeps the competition decent?

III.8.title: White silk first
III.8.reflection: Zixia asks about a line of an ode on a lovely smile and bright eyes on a plain ground. Confucius explains that colour is laid on after the white. Zixia leaps: so ritual comes after? The Master is pleased: now he can discuss the Odes with Shang, Zixia's personal name. Ritual is the colour; something plainer must come first.
III.8.question: What is the plain ground under your own good manners?

III.9.title: Not enough records
III.9.reflection: Confucius could describe the rites of the Xia and the Yin, he says, but the states descended from them, Qi and Song, do not keep enough documents or learned men to confirm him. If they did, he could prove what he says. He knows the difference between what he thinks and what he can show.
III.9.question: What do you believe that you could not prove?

III.10.title: After the libation
III.10.reflection: At the great sacrifice, once the libation has been poured, Confucius has no wish to watch any more. He does not say why. Most commentators think the rest of the rite was performed carelessly, or by a family with no right to it.
III.10.question: When have you stayed to watch something you no longer believed in?

III.11.title: The palm of the hand
III.11.reflection: Asked to explain the great sacrifice, Confucius says he does not know; whoever did would find governing the world as easy as looking at this, and he points to his palm. It is a refusal and a claim at once: the meaning of ritual, truly grasped, would be enough to order everything.
III.11.question: Is there a question you answer with "I do not know" because the true answer is too large?

III.12.title: As if present
III.12.reflection: He sacrificed to the dead as if they were present, and to the spirits as if they were present. If he could not take part himself, it was as though he had not sacrificed. The chapter describes an attitude rather than a belief: being fully there.
III.12.question: What do you do half-present that would change if you were there entirely?
III.12.exercise: Choose one ordinary task today and do it as if the person it is for were in the room.

III.13.title: The stove and the corner
III.13.reflection: Wangsun Jia, a powerful minister of Wei, quotes a proverb: better to court the god of the stove than the god of the south-west corner. It is a hint that Confucius should court the minister rather than the ruler. Confucius answers that whoever offends Heaven has no one left to pray to.
III.13.question: When were you advised to flatter the useful person rather than the right one?

III.14.title: I follow Zhou
III.14.reflection: The Zhou dynasty could look back on the two before it, and its culture is rich and elegant for that reason. Confucius follows Zhou. He chooses a tradition that had itself learned from earlier ones.
III.14.question: Which tradition do you follow, and what did it inherit before you received it?

III.15.title: Asking about everything
III.15.reflection: In the Grand Temple, Confucius asks about every detail, and someone sneers that the son of the man from Zou cannot know ritual. Hearing this, Confucius says: this is ritual. Asking, in a place where one is a guest, is itself correct conduct.
III.15.question: Where do you avoid asking for fear of looking ignorant?

III.16.title: Not piercing the hide
III.16.reflection: In ceremonial archery, piercing the target's leather is not the point, because people's strength differs. That was the old way. The contest measured form and accuracy, not force.
III.16.question: What do you measure yourself by that is really only a measure of strength?

III.17.title: You love the sheep
III.17.reflection: The sacrifice that announced the new moon had lapsed, but a sheep was still offered, and Zigong wanted to drop it. Confucius: you love the sheep, I love the ritual. As long as the sheep is offered, something of the rite survives to be restored.
III.17.question: What small remnant of a lapsed practice are you tempted to drop?

III.18.title: Called a flatterer
III.18.reflection: Serving one's ruler with full ritual is taken by others as flattery. In a court where the families ignored the forms, simply keeping them looked like fawning. Doing the correct thing can look like the wrong one from outside.
III.18.question: Have you been misread for doing something properly?

III.19.title: Ruler and minister
III.19.reflection: Duke Ding asks how a ruler should employ ministers and how ministers should serve. A ruler employs ministers by ritual; ministers serve the ruler with faithfulness, zhong. The relation runs both ways, and each side owes the other something.
III.19.question: In a relation where one person holds more power, what does the stronger one owe?

III.20.title: Joy without excess
III.20.reflection: The first poem of the Odes, the Guanju, has joy without wantonness and sorrow without injury. Confucius praises it for measure in feeling, not for the absence of feeling.
III.20.question: When did a strong feeling of yours stay within measure?

III.21.title: Done is done
III.21.reflection: Asked about the trees planted at the altars of the land, Zai Wo adds that the Zhou chose the chestnut to make the people tremble, a pun in Chinese. Confucius, hearing it, says: what is done need not be discussed, what is finished need not be argued, what is past need not be blamed. It reads as a rebuke that refuses to dwell.
III.21.question: What past mistake, yours or another's, would be better left without further blame?

III.22.title: The capacity of Guan Zhong
III.22.reflection: Confucius calls Guan Zhong, the famous minister of Qi, small in capacity. Was he frugal? No, he had three residences and staff who did one job each. Did he know ritual? He set up a gate screen and a cup stand as only rulers did. If he knew ritual, who does not? In XIV the same man is praised for what he achieved.
III.22.question: Can you think of someone who did great good and was small in their habits?

III.23.title: How music unfolds
III.23.reflection: Speaking to the music master of Lu, Confucius describes a piece: it begins with all parts together, then each is distinct yet in harmony, clear and flowing, until it ends. The description is a quiet model of how a group can work as well.
III.23.question: Where have you seen many people stay distinct and still move together?

III.24.title: The wooden bell
III.24.reflection: A border warden asks to meet Confucius and comes out consoling the disciples: why grieve over his loss of office? The world has long lacked the Way, and Heaven will use your master as a wooden-tongued bell, the kind officials rang to call the people to hear a proclamation. An outsider sees a vocation in the failure.
III.24.question: Has a setback of yours ever turned out to be a calling?

III.25.title: Beautiful and good
III.25.reflection: The Shao, the music of the sage king Shun, was perfectly beautiful and perfectly good. The Wu, music of King Wu who took the throne by conquest, was perfectly beautiful but not perfectly good. Beauty and goodness are judged separately, and a work can have one without the other.
III.25.question: What have you admired as beautiful that you could not call good?

III.26.title: What I cannot bear to watch
III.26.reflection: Holding high office without generosity, performing ritual without reverence, mourning without grief: how could Confucius look on such things? The book of ritual ends by naming three forms emptied of their content.
III.26.question: Which of these three have you seen, and which have you done?
